page: Amazon Web Services r6gd.8xlarge is a memory-optimized server instance powered by custom 64-bit ARM-based AWS Graviton processors. It features 32 dedicated physical cores using the Neoverse-N1 microarchitecture, operating at a clock speed of 2.5 GHz with a 1:1 vCPU-to-physical-core mapping. The instance is equipped with 256 GB of system memory, yielding a high memory-to-vCPU ratio of 8 GB per core. Local storage is provided via a bundled 1900 GB NVMe SSD instance store, and network performance is supported by a 12 Gbps baseline bandwidth on the AWS Nitro hypervisor.

Benchmark results place the r6gd.8xlarge in the average tier for most multi-core and memory operations. The instance achieved a multi-core stress-ng score of 48,584.58 and a Geekbench multi-core score of 11,391.0. Memory bandwidth tests show read-only speeds of 1894.04 GB/sec for cached small blocks and 150.22 GB/sec for uncached large blocks. However, single-core performance is a notable tradeoff, with Geekbench single-core scoring in the lower percentile at 933.0, and single-threaded bzip3 decompression registering poor performance at 6.62 GB/sec.

The ARM64 architecture of the Graviton processor delivers high resource density and qualitative cost-efficiency for memory-intensive workloads compared to traditional x86 alternatives. The combination of 256 GB RAM and 1900 GB of high-speed local NVMe storage makes this instance well-suited for memory-bound applications that require low-latency local scratch space. Appropriate workloads include relational and non-relational databases, in-memory caches such as Redis, data analytics, and medium-scale web serving.
description: Amazon Web Services r6gd.8xlarge is a memory-optimized, ARM64-based server instance powered by 32 dedicated AWS Graviton Neoverse-N1 physical cores running at 2.5 GHz. It features 256 GB of RAM, a bundled 1900 GB NVMe SSD local instance store, and a 12 Gbps baseline network bandwidth managed by the Nitro hypervisor. Benchmarks indicate solid multi-core and memory bandwidth capabilities, such as a multi-core Geekbench score of 11,391.0 and 38.98 million operations per second in Redis SET tests, though single-core performance remains a relative tradeoff. The high memory-to-vCPU ratio and fast local storage make this instance highly cost-efficient for memory-intensive databases, in-memory caching, and data processing workloads.
